fn.en: Speculate about the past; deduce what happened from a set of clues.

gr: must have, can’t have, might have and could have for deduction

acts.title: Text A · Four rules, no explanations
text: Every one of the following is a real rule, in a real company, and none of them came with a reason attached.

At a car plant in the north of England, all vehicles must be reversed into their spaces in the staff car park. At a law firm in London, employees are not permitted to take a lunch break away from the building. At a design agency in Dubai, work begins at six in the morning and ends at two. And at a software company in California, no drink of any kind may be brought within one metre of a desk.

Read like that, they sound arbitrary, and the staff who arrive on their first day usually assume they are. In every case they turned out not to be. The question is whether you can work out why before you read the second text.

items.q: What do the four rules have in common?
o: They are real, and none was explained to the staff
They were all invented as a joke
They all come from the same company

items.q: What does the writer say about new staff?
o: They usually assume the rules are arbitrary
They are told the reasons on day one

acts.title: Text B · Four reasons, found afterwards
text: The car park rule is about safety. If every car is already facing outwards, nobody has to reverse into a crowd of people leaving at the end of a shift. Accidents in that car park fell by two thirds.
The law firm’s rule looks harsh, and it was: clients count on reaching their lawyer, and somebody had to answer the phones. The firm was criticized for it in the press and quietly changed it.
Dubai is obvious once you have been there in July. The hours were moved to avoid the heat, and staff go home before the worst of it.
The software rule is the least interesting and the most expensive. Somebody must have spilt a drink over a machine — and, judging by the metre, more than one somebody.

items.s: The car park rule was introduced for safety reasons.
Accidents in the car park went up after the rule.
The law firm kept its lunch rule after being criticized.
The Dubai hours were changed because of the heat.
The writer is certain why the software rule exists.
The writer thinks a drink was probably spilt on a machine.

acts.title: Look again at Text B
text: Somebody must have spilt a drink over a machine.
It must have been a way of making the car park safer.
Surely they can’t have stopped them having a lunch break.
It might have been a safety issue.
I suppose it could have been something like that.
They may have needed people to stay and answer the phones.

items.q: “Somebody must have spilt a drink.” How sure is the writer?
“They can’t have stopped them having a lunch break.” What does this mean?
o: The speaker is almost certain it did not happen

items.q: “It might have been a safety issue.” How sure?
What is the form in all six sentences?

acts.title: Deduction about the past
rule: When you are working out what happened, English does not use the past tense. It uses a present modal plus have plus a past participle. The modal carries how sure you are; the have + participle carries the fact that it is in the past.
points: You are almost certain it DID happen, and you can point to the evidence.
You are almost certain it did NOT happen. This is the opposite of must have, and it is the form to use in British English.
might have / may have / could have
It is one possibility among several. These three are interchangeable here.
modal + have + past participle, whatever the subject. He must have gone, they must have gone.
eg: Somebody must have spilt a drink on it.
Almost certain — there is a rule about drinks.
It must have been a safety issue.
Almost certain, from the evidence.
They can’t have stopped them having lunch.
Almost certain it did not happen.
She can’t have known about the meeting.
Not “mustn’t have known”.
It might have been the heat.
One possibility.
They may have needed somebody to answer the phones.
Another possibility, equally weighted.
I suppose it could have been something like that.
Softest of all, and very common in speech.
He must have been working late — the light is still on.
must have been + -ing, for an activity in progress.
They can’t have been friends.
can’t have been, for a past state.
He might have been made redundant.
Passive: modal + have + been + past participle.
acts.careful: In British English the negative of must for deduction is can’t: “They can’t have known.” American English also allows “must not have known”, but mustn’t have is not used in Britain in this meaning, and in a British exam it will be marked wrong.

items.q: The light is still on, so he ___ working late.
Surely they ___ them having a lunch break.
It ___ a safety issue, but nobody is sure.
Somebody ___ a drink over the machine.
He ___ redundant — the department closed.
She ___ about the meeting. Nobody told her.

acts.title: From what you can see to what you can say
steps: The car park has almost no accidents in it.
Start with the evidence you actually have.
1 · Say what you think happened, in plain past tense.
2 · Choose the modal for how sure you are. Almost certain → must.
3 · Add HAVE. This is what puts it in the past.
Somebody must have thought about safety.
4 · Add the PAST PARTICIPLE. Never the past simple: not “must have thought about” → “must thought”.

items.q: Evidence: the office is empty at 4 p.m. → They ___ early.
Evidence: she has never mentioned it → She ___ about it.
Evidence: there are two possible explanations → It ___ the heat.
Evidence: his coat is wet → He ___ in the rain.

lines: The first rule sounds ridiculous. It [must have been|must be|must have be] a way of making the car park safer.
Surely they [can’t have stopped|mustn’t have stopped|couldn’t stopped] them having a lunch break.
They [may have needed|may need then|may have need] people to stay and answer the phones.
The third one seems fair. It [might have been|might be|might have be] a hot country.
Someone [must have spilt|must spill|must have spill] a drink over a computer — and the machine [can’t have survived|mustn’t have survived|can’t survived] it.

items.from: I am almost certain somebody spilt a drink on it.

steps.a: Somebody must have spilt a drink on it

steps.cue: Now make it a possibility instead, with MIGHT
steps.a: Somebody might have spilt a drink on it

items.from: I am almost certain they did not stop the lunch break.

steps.a: They can’t have stopped the lunch break

steps.cue: Now soften it to a possibility with MAY NOT
steps.a: They may not have stopped the lunch break

items.from: The light was on all evening. I think he was working.

steps.cue: Say it with MUST and a continuous form
steps.why: must have been + -ing describes an activity in progress in the past.

steps.cue: Now say the opposite is impossible, with CAN’T
steps.a: He can’t have been at home

items.from: It is not necessary for staff to reverse into the spaces.

steps.cue: Rewrite it in the present with DON’T HAVE TO
steps.a: Staff don’t have to reverse into the spaces
alt: Staff do not have to reverse into the spaces
steps.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 5 — and notice that this is obligation, not deduction.

steps.cue: Now say the rule is forbidden to break, with MUSTN’T

use: I suppose it could have been…

write.q: Think of a rule at your work, your school or in your building that nobody has ever explained to you. Write about 150 words speculating about why it exists. Use must have at least once, can’t have at least once, and might have or could have at least twice. Then say which explanation you actually believe.
plan: the explanation you are almost sure of
one you are almost sure is wrong
write.model:
In our building nobody is allowed to use the lift between eight and nine in the morning, and no notice anywhere explains why.

It must have been a decision taken after something went wrong, because the sign is handwritten and the tape holding it up has gone yellow. Nothing that specific gets written by accident.

It can’t have been about weight. The lift takes eight people and the sign says nothing about numbers, only about the hour.

It might have been an energy measure, although that would be an odd hour to choose. It could equally have been a maintenance window that somebody forgot to remove.

My own guess is that somebody must have got stuck in it during the morning rush, and that the rule is a very cheap way of making sure it does not happen twice.
